newsitem.title: POLAND: POLISH REFERENDUM VERDICT A SETBACK FOR SOLIDARITY.
newsitem.headline: POLISH REFERENDUM VERDICT A SETBACK FOR SOLIDARITY.

text.p: Exit poll results showing a victory for Poland's new constitution in a referendum on Sunday were an ominous sign for the rightist opposition as it prepares to challenge the ruling ex-communists in elections this year.

Many analysts saw the referendum as a trial of strength between the ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance, which helped draft the charter, and the opposition Solidarity Election Action (AWS) before parliamentary polls due around September.
"The referendum has to a large extent been a test of strength," sociologist Edmund Wnuk-Lipinski told Reuters.
"Solidarity's...defeat shows it may have difficulty mobilising part of its electorate," he said.

Exit polls, released by public television, indicated 56.8 percent voted "yes" for the constitution, 43.2 percent were against and the turnout was 39.8 percent of the 28 million voters. Official results are due late on Monday or on Tuesday.

Recent opinion polls show the AWS and the ex-communists each enjoy similar support of more than one fifth of potential voters, which under Poland's electoral system would translate into about one third of votes in the 460-seat parliament.

Surveys also indicate the AWS, a bloc of more than 30 small parties led by the Solidarity union, has more potential to enlarge its support, because a many Poles still despise the ruling party's roots in the oppressive system before 1989.

But the referendum outcome appears to show Solidarity's campaign rhetoric, which in the case of the constitution relied more on vague patriotic and religious values and strong anti-communism than specific arguments, had limited appeal.

"Solidarity's...defeat may largely be due to its dramatic tone, which is unsuitable for the current reality. We saw an appeal to emotions and not to reason and most people do not get carried away just by emotions," said Wnuk-Lipinski.
Solidarity leaders accused the constitution of betraying national interests by allegedly allowing Poland to surrender by treaty some functions to international organisations.
They also said the charter should be rejected because it did not clearly invoke God and include a clause effectively banning abortion, now legal in Poland.

Last month, some top Solidarity leaders asked the Church to seek God's help in defeating the constitution by performing a ceremony of "Enthroning Christ the King" -- a step last taken as Bolshevik troops invaded Poland in 1920.
The Church refused, but the episode was a gift to Solidarity's critics and was widely ridiculed as hyperbole.

"They (Solidarity) abuse references to God and the Church in their campaign. People, even their own supporters, do not like it...this is one reason for the defeat," said Andrzej Potocki, spokesman for the opposition Union for Freedom party.

Potocki's centrist party was one of the opposition groups which clinched a constitutional compromise with the ruling coalition of ex-communists and a Peasant party, after years of hot debate, and helped pass the charter in parliament.

The party argued that it was better to have an imperfect constitution than stay with remnants of the 1952, Stalin-era one, amended in 1992 by interim laws, which would leave Poland as the only former Soviet bloc country without a new charter.
The Union for Freedom, along with the Peasants and the rightist Movement for the Reconstruction of Poland, is one of several smaller groups which may hold the balance of power in the next parliament.

Although the referendum verdict means the constitution will now take effect in just over three months, the constitutional debate will not end, with the Solidarity officials declaring they will change it if they win the September elections.
"Controversial points in this constitution will have to be corrected in the future parliament," Jacek Rybicki, Solidarity's senior official, said after the exit poll results.
He said the referendum verdict could not be seen as a victory for the left because the turnout had been so low. -- Warsaw Newsroom +48 22 653 9700
